title: Tiered Error-Budget Safety-Net Patterns and Runbook
author: Aisha Khan
body:
Summary:

This page documents the Tiered Error-Budget Safety-Net design pattern, associated capacity planning guidance, operational tooling integrations, and an actionable SRE runbook for managing high-consumption error budgets across multi-tenant inference services. The pattern is intended to reduce blast radius, keep critical customers online, and defer costly capacity purchases while enforcing reliability commitments.

Scope and audience:
- SREs responsible for inference-serving SLOs and multi-tenant capacity governance
- Platform/product owners defining SLO contracts for tenants
- Incident commanders and oncall engineers who execute capacity and throttling actions

Problem statement:
As inference workloads become more heterogeneous, single-threshold error-budget triggers either overreact (unnecessary capacity spend) or underreact (missed mitigations). A tiered safety-net provides graduated mitigations mapped to business impact and tenancy class.

Design overview (pattern):
1) Define orthogonal SLOs and error budgets per product surface (generation, embeddings, chat). Typical SLOs we enforce:
   - Availability SLO (successful 2xx token-stream responses): 99.95% over 30d for critical tenants; 99.5% for standard tenants.
   - Latency SLO (p95 tail for token completion): <200ms for interactive, <500ms for batch embeddings.
   - Quality guardrail (regression counts relative to eval prompt-set): <=1.0% regression rate month-over-month.
2) Create tier buckets for tenants and internal payload classes:
   - Tier A (critical, enterprise SLA)
   - Tier B (paid, high-volume)
   - Tier C (free/self-serve)
3) Establish a three-stage safety-net mapped to percent of monthly error-budget consumed:
   - Advisory (>=30% consumed): notifications, suggested knob recommendations, additional telemetry collection.
   - Protective (>=70% consumed): soft preemption of lowest-priority requests, enable conservative batching heuristics, spin up elastic reserved nodes.
   - Emergency (>=100% consumed or sustained burn-rate > 10%/hour): aggressive throttling, tenant-level cost-cutoff, auto-failover to cheaper model variant or region.

Operational knobs and capacity actions (examples):
- Autoscale: reserve +10–30% burst capacity via dedicated GPU pool when protective stage triggers.
- Throttles: apply token-priority gating to deprioritize Tier C requests (see runbook step 4).
- Fallbacks: route heavy requests to quantized model variants (e.g., 4-bit QAT) with documented latency/quality tradeoffs.

SLO examples and math (reference):
- Example Availability SLO (API v1 generation): 99.95% over 30d -> allowed unavailability per 30d = 0.05% of 30d = 0.0005 * 30 * 24 * 60 = 21.6 minutes.
- Error budget burn-rate threshold: protective at 70% -> remaining budget = 6.48 minutes.
- If burn-rate > 10%/hour for 3 consecutive hours, escalate to emergency.

Capacity planning tie-ins:
- Headroom bands: planned headroom = 25% for Tier A-dominated clusters, 45% for mixed clusters.
- Onboarding runway: new tenant onboarding plan must include a 90-day traffic forecast, synthetic canary profiles, and an initial dedicated headroom of 15% for the first 30 days.
- Elastic reservoir policy: maintain a global pool able to absorb 15% of average 30d peak token throughput; policy owner: capacity-team@sre.redwood.com.

Tiered safety-net decision table (quick reference):
| Error budget consumed | Immediate action | Owner | Telemetry to collect | Escalation window |
|-----------------------|------------------|-------|---------------------|-------------------|
| 0–30%                 | Advisory notifications; add sampling | Service Owner | p95 latency, 5xx rate, queue depth | N/A |
| 30–70%                | Apply conservative batching; enable more aggressive prefix cache | Platform SRE | CPU/GPU utilization, KV hit-rate | 6 hours |
| 70–100%               | Start elastic reserved pool; soft-prioritization of tokens | Oncall SRE | Headroom, dropped tokens | 1 hour |
| >=100%                | Throttle non-critical tenants; route to fallback models; incident declared | Incident Commander | All telemetry + request traces | Immediate |

Runbook: Tiered Error-Budget Safety-Net (step-by-step)
1) Detection (automated):
   - Prometheus rule: slo_budget_burn_rate{service="inference-api"} > 0.10 for 1h -> fire "errbud_high_burn" alert.
   - PagerDuty routing: alert to Platform SRE primary, with on-call escalation to Incident Commander if protective stage is reached.
2) Initial triage (15 minutes):
   1. Confirm the alert and review anchor dashboards (SLO heatmap, per-tenant burn charts, p95 latency).
   2. Identify which tenants and routes are driving burn.
   3. Check recent deploys (CI/CD tags) and infra events (node churn, GPU OOMs).
3) Advisory actions (if >=30%):
   - Notify service owners with recommended knobs: increase batch size by +10%, extend prefix cache TTL, enable token-priority sampling on non-critical routes.
   - Turn on enhanced tracing for top 5 offenders for 60 minutes.
4) Protective actions (if >=70%):
   - Execute: srectl capacity reserve --pool elastic-reservoir --percent 20 --reason "protective error-budget"
   - Apply token-priority gating policy: POST /internal/priority-gate {"tenant_filter":"tier!=A","max_qps":0.8} (example CLI shown in internal API docs).
   - Deploy fallback routing rule: route /v1/embeddings heavy->quantized-embed-v0.8.
5) Emergency actions (if >=100% or sustained high burn):
   - Declare incident and set priority to Sev2 (or Sev1 if customer impact observed).
   - Initiate aggressive tenant throttling: runbook command: srectl throttle tenant --selector "tier:C" --mode soft-fail 60m.
   - Cross-region failover: if region-level saturation, execute region-failover checklist in /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/cross-cluster-failover-execution-and-verification-playbook-2025.
6) Post-incident and remediation (within 72 hours):
   - Create incident review with hypothesis, evidence, mitigations, and a remediation owner. Use the Incident Evidence Checklist below.
   - If action included capacity reservation, assess cost and purpose; attach cost estimate to remediation ticket.

Incident Evidence Checklist (minimum):
- SLO heatmap snapshot (30d and 7d)
- Per-tenant burn chart with raw request traces for top 5 offenders
- Node-level telemetry (GPU utilization, OOM logs, disk pressure) for impacted timeframe
- CI/CD deploy log around time-of-onset with commit hashes
- PagerDuty/timeline export and command audit (who ran srectl)

Operational tooling integrations and automation recipes:
- Telemetry: Prometheus -> Thanos for long-term retention; tenant-scoped metrics prefixed slo_budget_* and tenant_id label.
- Alerting: Grafana Alerting with direct PagerDuty escalation for protective/emergency stages.
- Control plane CLI: srectl (homegrown) supports capacity reserve, throttle, and priority-gate operations. Example: srectl capacity reserve --help
  - Key commands used in safety-net:
    - srectl capacity reserve --pool <pool> --percent <n> --reason <txt>
    - srectl throttle tenant --selector "tenant:<id>" --mode <soft|hard> --duration <m>
    - srectl rollback model --service inference-api --to-tag <model-tag>
- Audit logs: all srectl operations are forwarded to the audit-log service and archived per compliance retention.

Runbook playbook snippets (CLI + PromQL)
- PromQL (protective stage):
  sum by (tenant_id) (increase(slo_budget_consumed_total{service="inference-api"}[1h])) / sum by (tenant_id) (slo_budget_total{service="inference-api"}) > 0.7
- Example srectl sequence for protective stage:
  1) srectl capacity reserve --pool elastic-reservoir --percent 20 --reason "protective error-budget"
  2) srectl priority-gate apply --selector "tier!=A" --max-qps 80
  3) curl -X POST "http://internal-router/route" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"route":"/v1/embeddings","target":"quantized-embed-v0.8"}'

Postmortem and remediation gating:
- If emergency actions were taken, the incident owner must open a remediation RFC within 5 business days that includes: cost impact, proposed permanent mitigations (capacity or software), and a timeline.
- Remediation priority is determined by SLA exposure and business impact; tickets are tracked in the Reliability Initiative board with labels: slo-remediation, capacity, cost-impact.

Ownership and roles:
- Platform SRE: maintains global safety-net automation and elastic-reservoir policies.
- Service Owner: owns tenant SLO definitions, quality monitors, and primary communication with customers.
- Incident Commander: declares incidents and authorizes emergency throttles.
- Capacity Team: approves large (>30%) reserved capacity allocations and performs cost reconciliation.

Governance and periodic review:
- Quarterly SLO review: every quarter owners must validate SLOs and tier assignments; test safety-net actions in a simulated canary (chaos) window.
- Annual capacity stress test: execute a 48-hour surge exercise against a replicated test cluster to verify elastic-reservoir plumbing, throttles, and failover.

Appendix 
- Known quality tradeoffs when routing to quantized fallback models: measured embedding cosine drift ~0.7–1.5% on curated eval sets; p95 latency reduction 20–40%.
- Contact list: capacity-team@sre.redwood.com, platform-oncall@sre.redwood.com

Change log:
- 2027-11-05: Created by Aisha Khan (initial draft)
- 2028-03-14: Added protective/emergency commands, clarified PROMQL and incident evidence checklist (reviewers: Miguel Santos, Rina Patel, Owen Li)

References:
- SLO definition and admission playbook: /confluence/eng-sre/capacity-planning/service-onboarding-runway-and-slo-admission-playbook-2026
- Cross-cluster failover runbook: /confluence/eng-sre/runbooks/cross-cluster-failover-execution-and-verification-playbook-2025
- Token-priority and throttling APis: /confluence/eng-sre/operational-tooling/token-priority-capacity-arbitration-field-manual-2027

If you have a new tenant or see a pattern that doesn't fit the tiers above, open an RFC and tag it slo-exception-request so we can evaluate the correct safety-net placement.
